prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form that made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The scientific case is a complete arc from hormone physiology (secretion, the incretin effect, the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, DPP-4 degradation) to receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, and then to drugs with large outcome-trial evidence in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism has been confirmed independently for decades, so there is no maturity problem. A prize built on Holst (physiology), Drucker (biology and therapeutic concept) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active peptide) honours the discovery layer, which is the layer the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has traditionally rewarded, and it keeps the citation tied to a physiological finding rather than to a product.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for the active peptide is contested, with Habener-group work and Mojsov's role not cleanly separable from the supplied record, and a three-person cap excludes Knudsen, whose medicinal chemistry produced the long-acting agonists that actually reached patients. A prize that omits the drug developers may look like it rewards the story of the discovery more than the reason the discovery matters. A committee that cannot defend Mojsov over Knudsen, or over an uncredited early contributor, risks an unstable attribution. I also note that all six of us converging on one candidate may reflect shared reasoning from the same evidence, not independent confirmation.

responses.point: The chair proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. He considers Knudsen the leading figure in the medicinal chemistry behind liraglutide and semaglutide, and he considers Mojsov's weight contested.
responses.response: I take the Knudsen argument seriously, and it is the best alternative trio. I still prefer Mojsov. The identification of the active peptide is a discovery-stage finding that made everything downstream possible, while the long-acting analogues are a development achievement that can be recognised by a separate prize or a later arrangement. I agree with the chair that Mojsov's weight is contested, but a contested priority claim in the record is not a reason to drop her unless someone can show that the active-form work is overstated. If the committee cannot settle that, I would rather say so openly than replace her by default.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked GLP-1 first with Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. He judged Knudsen's work to be drug development better suited to a different recognition, and he put the unfolded protein response (B043) second.
responses.response: I agree with his trio and with his reading of Knudsen. I disagree with putting B043 second. The unfolded protein response is a clean and original discovery with a very stable mechanism. However, its disease and therapeutic relevance is still being worked out. Next to the work on CAR-T cells and on antisense therapy for spinal muscular atrophy, it has a weaker link to human physiology and medicine. In the opening round I put it fourth, so this is a question of weighting, not of scientific quality.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius supports CAR-T (B015) as a strong second choice but says that leaving out Zelig Eshhar, who is not among the credited names, weakens a fair allocation.
responses.response: I share this concern and it is the main reason I would not make B015 my first-choice prize this year. The chimeric receptor concept originated outside the credited set, and I cannot see how a trio of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg avoids a misleading citation. Where I differ is that I do not think this should delay a prize for CAR-T. If the committee decides it wants a second part, the question is whether the citation can be written for the clinical and engineering contributions without implying that the concept originated with those three. I think that is possible but only barely, and I would want to see the wording.

responses.point: El Manira ranked optogenetics (B036) second, with Deisseroth, Nagel and Bamberg, and notes that the three-person cap leaves out decisive contributors.
responses.response: I respect the scientific case for optogenetics, but I am not persuaded it competes with GLP-1 or CAR-T on impact on human health. It is a transformative research tool, and the attribution problem is the worst on the shortlist, with six credited names, contested priority between channelrhodopsin discovery and neuronal application, and Miesenböck's earlier work. I would not choose among those six unless we were willing to leave out at least three people we agree are decisive. That is a significant risk to the credibility of the prize.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 peptide is distinct enough from Habener-group work to justify a place over Knudsen.
Whether the committee prefers to honour the physiology or the drug development, and whether a second part for drug development would be justified within the three-person cap.
Whether the credited names for CAR-T can support a citation that does not misstate the origin of the concept given Eshhar's absence.
Long-term safety of chronic incretin use is still accruing and I have not verified the details of the priority dispute.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the provided profile. My spatial transcriptomics and single-cell work is not connected to any shortlisted candidate, and I recorded co-authorships with colleagues on the committee, which do not involve any shortlisted candidate or credited name.
